title: Dimensional modeling & Power BI
blurb: Grain, fact types, conformed dimensions and the DAX semantics behind a shared semantic model.

cards.prompt: Kimball's four steps of dimensional design, in order.
cards.answer: 1. Select the business process. 2. Declare the grain. 3. Identify the dimensions. 4. Identify the facts.
cards.source: Kimball & Ross, The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 3rd ed.

cards.prompt: What does 'declare the grain' mean, and what goes wrong if you skip it?
cards.answer: State exactly what one fact row represents, for example one row per service request per status change. Skip it and grains get mixed in one table, which causes double counting and measures that are right only at some levels of aggregation.
points: Grain = the business meaning of one row
Declared before dimensions and facts are chosen
Mixed grains lead to double counting and inconsistent measures

cards.prompt: Pothole lifecycle (reported, dispatched, repaired, inspected), with one row per pothole whose date columns fill in over time. Which fact-table type?
cards.why: Transaction: one row per event. Periodic snapshot: one row per period (open requests at month end). Accumulating snapshot: one row per process instance, updated as milestones occur. It's the natural home for durations like time-to-dispatch.

cards.prompt: Slowly changing dimension Types 1, 2 and 3, one line each.
cards.answer: Type 1: overwrite (no history). Type 2: add a new row with effective dates and a current flag (full history). Type 3: add a previous-value column (one step of history).

cards.prompt: What are a conformed dimension and a bus matrix, and why do they matter across departments?
cards.answer: A conformed dimension has the same keys and meaning everywhere it is used, such as one Address, Date or Department dimension. That lets you drill across business processes. A bus matrix lists processes as rows and conformed dimensions as columns. It is the roadmap that keeps department models compatible with each other.
points: Same keys and meaning across fact tables
Bus matrix = processes by shared dimensions, the integration plan

cards.prompt: In DAX, how do row context and filter context differ, and what does CALCULATE do with a row context?
cards.answer: Row context is iteration row by row (calculated columns, iterators like SUMX), and on its own it filters nothing. Filter context is the set of filters on the model (slicers, visuals, CALCULATE arguments). CALCULATE performs context transition: it turns the current row context into an equivalent filter context.
points: Filter context = filters on the model
CALCULATE converts row context to filter context (context transition)
cards.source: Russo & Ferrari, The Definitive Guide to DAX (SQLBI)

cards.prompt: Why does Power BI's engine favor a star schema over one wide flat table or a deep snowflake?
cards.answer: VertiPaq stores data by column, so low-cardinality dimension columns compress well, and dimensions filter facts through one-to-many relationships. A wide flat table repeats attributes and invites inconsistent measures and grain errors. A deep snowflake adds relationship hops and confuses report authors.
points: Columnar compression favors low-cardinality dimension columns
Dimensions filter facts via one-to-many relationships
Flat tables: repetition, grain errors, inconsistent measures
Snowflakes: extra hops and author confusion
cards.source: Microsoft Learn: Star schema guidance for Power BI

cards.prompt: What is the default cross-filter direction for a one-to-many relationship in Power BI, and what's the risk of switching it to 'both'?
cards.answer: Single: the one side filters the many side. Bidirectional filtering can create ambiguous filter paths and slower queries. Keep relationships single and enable bidirectional filtering per measure (CROSSFILTER) or use TREATAS.

cards.prompt: A department wants 'one big flat table' in Power BI so staff can self-serve. What do you recommend, and how do you sell it?
cards.answer: Name the risks: mixed grains, double counting, and every report reinventing its measures. Offer a shared semantic model instead: a star schema with a few conformed dimensions and curated measures. One certified dataset then feeds many reports. Teach staff to build reports on that model rather than their own extracts. Sell it with a before-and-after on their own numbers, ideally a total that comes out differently today depending on who built the report.
points: Name the risks: grain, double counting, inconsistent measures
Propose a shared semantic model (star, conformed dimensions, curated measures)
One certified dataset feeds many reports
Train report building on the shared model
